title: CTS Psalms — Unit 3: Psalm 24, The King of Glory

blocks.en: 📖 The Book of Psalms — Unit 3: Psalm 24, The King of Glory
blocks.es_reference: 📖 El Libro de los Salmos — Unidad 3: Salmo 24, El Rey de Gloria

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "The earth is the Lord's, and all its fullness, the world and those who dwell therein." — Psalm 24:1 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "De Jehová es la tierra y su plenitud; el mundo, y los que en él habitan." — Salmo 24:1 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. David Brings the Ark to Jerusalem
blocks.es_reference: 1. David lleva el Arca a Jerusalén

blocks.en: The story behind this psalm is given to us in 2 Samuel chapter 6 — the story of King David bringing the Ark of the Covenant up to the city of Jerusalem. Ever since Moses, the ark had represented the presence of God in the midst of His people. During the wars with the Philistines it had been captured, then returned, and for some twenty years it had been kept in the house of a man named Abinadab. Now David had been made king over all Israel, had captured the Jebusite town we call Jerusalem, and wanted his new capital to be not only the political center of the kingdom but its worship center as well. So he set out to bring the ark home.
blocks.es_reference: La historia detrás de este salmo se nos da en 2 Samuel capítulo 6 — la historia del rey David llevando el Arca del Pacto a la ciudad de Jerusalén. Desde Moisés, el arca había representado la presencia de Dios en medio de Su pueblo. Durante las guerras con los filisteos había sido capturada, luego devuelta, y por unos veinte años había estado en la casa de un hombre llamado Abinadab. Ahora David había sido hecho rey sobre todo Israel, había tomado la ciudad jebusea que llamamos Jerusalén, y quería que su nueva capital fuera no solo el centro político del reino sino también su centro de adoración. Así que se propuso llevar el arca a casa.

blocks.en: The story is one of trial and error. The first attempt failed. The ark was being hauled on an ox cart when the oxen stumbled, and a man named Uzzah reached out to steady it and died on the spot. David was both angry and afraid, and the mission stopped right there; the ark was taken to the house of Obed-Edom, where the LORD blessed him for three months. The second attempt succeeded. This time David and the whole house of Israel brought the ark up with shouts and trumpets, and David, wearing a linen ephod, danced before the LORD with all his might. For this occasion David wrote a hymn to be sung as the ark came up — Psalm 24.
blocks.es_reference: La historia es de ensayo y error. El primer intento fracasó. El arca era llevada en una carreta de bueyes cuando los bueyes tropezaron, y un hombre llamado Uza extendió la mano para sostenerla y murió en el acto. David quedó enojado y temeroso, y la misión se detuvo allí mismo; el arca fue llevada a la casa de Obed-Edom, donde Jehová lo bendijo por tres meses. El segundo intento tuvo éxito. Esta vez David y toda la casa de Israel subieron el arca con gritos y trompetas, y David, vestido de un efod de lino, danzó delante de Jehová con todas sus fuerzas. Para esta ocasión David escribió un himno para cantarse mientras subía el arca — el Salmo 24.

blocks.en: 2. The One Great Question
blocks.es_reference: 2. La Gran Pregunta

blocks.en: Psalm 24:1 (NKJV): "The earth is the LORD's, and all its fullness, the world and those who dwell therein. For He has founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the waters."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 24:1 (RVG): "De Jehová es la tierra y su plenitud; el mundo, y los que en él habitan. Porque él la fundó sobre los mares, y la afirmó sobre los ríos."

blocks.en: Within these short ten verses there are two important questions, and the most important of them is this one, asked twice: "Who is this King of glory?" The psalm answers it three ways — He is the Owner of the earth, He is the Judge who decides who may stand in His holy place, and He is "the LORD strong and mighty." David answers his own question by showing us the King's World, the King's Worship, and the King's Welcome. If we will follow him through all three, we will learn how to welcome our King.
blocks.es_reference: Dentro de estos breves diez versículos hay dos preguntas importantes, y la más importante es esta, hecha dos veces: "¿Quién es este Rey de gloria?" El salmo la responde de tres maneras — Él es el Dueño de la tierra, Él es el Juez que decide quién puede estar en Su lugar santo, y Él es "Jehová fuerte y valiente." David responde su propia pregunta mostrándonos el Mundo del Rey, la Adoración del Rey, y la Bienvenida del Rey. Si lo seguimos por las tres, aprenderemos cómo dar la bienvenida a nuestro Rey.

blocks.en: 3. The King's World
blocks.es_reference: 3. El Mundo del Rey

blocks.en: The first answer is that this King owns everything. "The earth is the LORD's, and all its fullness." God is not some good-luck charm we carry in our pocket to ward off trouble and guarantee success. He is the Owner of all things and all people. He created the earth, gathered the seas, formed the dry land, and as its Creator He knows what blessings He wants to give and how and when He wants to give them. Sometimes people get the idea that mankind has been handed the earth to do with as we please. But we are not the owners of the earth; we are only the tenant farmers, caring for the land for the Owner. Whatever we do, we are like servants who are accountable to the Master for how we treat His property. Joseph was a steward of Potiphar's house, and he was faithful in it.
blocks.es_reference: La primera respuesta es que este Rey posee todo. "De Jehová es la tierra y su plenitud." Dios no es un amuleto de buena suerte que llevamos en el bolsillo para ahuyentar los problemas y garantizar el éxito. Él es el Dueño de todas las cosas y de todas las personas. Creó la tierra, reunió los mares, formó la tierra seca, y como su Creador sabe qué bendiciones quiere dar y cómo y cuándo quiere darlas. A veces la gente cree que a la humanidad se le ha entregado la tierra para hacer con ella lo que quiera. Pero no somos los dueños de la tierra; somos solo los labradores arrendatarios, cuidando la tierra para el Dueño. Hagamos lo que hagamos, somos como siervos que rinden cuentas al Amo por cómo tratamos Su propiedad. José fue mayordomo de la casa de Potifar, y fue fiel en ello.

blocks.en: Jesus told of an owner who planted a vineyard, built a wall and a watchtower to guard it, and dug a winepress, then rented it out to tenant farmers (Matthew 21:33). Bill Carlson wrote a whole book, The Sharecropper, on this idea. A sharecropper is a tenant who works land he does not own; the landowner buys the seed, the tools, the stock, and the worker gets a share of the crop. We are like that before God. He owns everything and cares for us. As Paul says in 1 Timothy 6:7, "we brought nothing into the world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out." When we need anything, we simply turn to God, who was here long before we came and will be here long after we are gone.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús habló de un dueño que plantó una viña, edificó una cerca y una torre para guardarla, y cavó un lagar, y luego la arrendó a labradores (Mateo 21:33). Bill Carlson escribió todo un libro, The Sharecropper (El Aparcero), sobre esta idea. Un aparcero es un arrendatario que trabaja una tierra que no posee; el dueño compra la semilla, las herramientas, el ganado, y el trabajador recibe una parte de la cosecha. Así somos nosotros delante de Dios. Él posee todo y cuida de nosotros. Como dice Pablo en 1 Timoteo 6:7: "nada hemos traído a este mundo, y sin duda nada podremos sacar." Cuando necesitamos algo, simplemente acudimos a Dios, que estaba aquí mucho antes de que llegáramos y estará aquí mucho después de que nos vayamos.

blocks.en: 4. Stealing What Belongs to God
blocks.es_reference: 4. Robar lo que Pertenece a Dios

blocks.en: Our number-one responsibility as His tenant farmers is to tell other people about the Lord. But there is a sober warning attached to forgetting whose world this is. Do you remember the story of Achan? When the walls of Jericho came tumbling down, Achan saw in the ruins a beautiful robe from Babylon, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold, and he coveted them, took them, and hid them in the ground under his tent (Joshua 7). Israel then lost the next battle, because someone had taken what belonged to God. The Lord told Joshua that Israel had sinned, and the guilty party was found out, tribe by tribe and family by family, until Achan was taken. He confessed, and he and his household were stoned to death.
blocks.es_reference: Nuestra responsabilidad número uno como Sus labradores arrendatarios es hablar a otros del Señor. Pero hay una solemne advertencia ligada a olvidar de quién es este mundo. ¿Recuerda la historia de Acán? Cuando los muros de Jericó se derrumbaron, Acán vio en las ruinas un hermoso manto de Babilonia, doscientos siclos de plata y una barra de oro, y los codició, los tomó y los escondió en la tierra debajo de su tienda (Josué 7). Israel perdió entonces la siguiente batalla, porque alguien había tomado lo que pertenecía a Dios. El Señor dijo a Josué que Israel había pecado, y el culpable fue descubierto, tribu por tribu y familia por familia, hasta que Acán fue señalado. Confesó, y él y su casa fueron apedreados hasta morir.

blocks.en: Why such a harsh penalty? Because the things Achan took belonged to God. He had stolen from God Himself. If the world is the Lord's, then to grasp it for ourselves as though we were the owners is no small thing. And the lesson runs the other way too: if the world is the Lord's, then He is worthy of our worship. That brings us to the second answer.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Por qué un castigo tan severo? Porque lo que Acán tomó pertenecía a Dios. Había robado a Dios mismo. Si el mundo es del Señor, entonces aferrarlo para nosotros como si fuéramos los dueños no es cosa pequeña. Y la lección corre también al revés: si el mundo es del Señor, entonces Él es digno de nuestra adoración. Eso nos lleva a la segunda respuesta.

blocks.en: 5. The King's Worship
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Adoración del Rey

blocks.en: Psalm 24:3-5 (NKJV): "Who may ascend into the hill of the LORD? Or who may stand in His holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who has not lifted up his soul to an idol, nor sworn deceitfully. He shall receive blessing from the LORD."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 24:3-5 (RVG): "¿Quién subirá al monte de Jehová? ¿Y quién estará en su lugar santo? El limpio de manos y puro de corazón; el que no ha elevado su alma a la vanidad, ni jurado con engaño. Recibirá bendición de Jehová."

blocks.en: God is holy, and He expects us to approach Him in holiness. David had apparently prepared the Levites for the task of carrying the ark, but he had learned during that first, failed attempt that holiness could not be taken lightly — that was part of the explanation for Uzzah's death. Clean hands and a pure heart are the password at the door. When the wise men saw His star in the east, they came to worship Him. When a woman who had lived a sinful life learned that Jesus was eating at the Pharisee's house, she came with an alabaster jar of perfume, stood behind Him weeping, wet His feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and poured the perfume on Him. That woman came to worship Jesus. Worship is the response of a clean heart to a holy King.
blocks.es_reference: Dios es santo, y espera que nos acerquemos a Él en santidad. David aparentemente había preparado a los levitas para la tarea de cargar el arca, pero había aprendido durante aquel primer intento fallido que la santidad no podía tomarse a la ligera — esa fue parte de la explicación de la muerte de Uza. Manos limpias y corazón puro son la contraseña en la puerta. Cuando los magos vieron Su estrella en el oriente, vinieron a adorarle. Cuando una mujer que había llevado una vida pecaminosa supo que Jesús comía en casa del fariseo, vino con un frasco de alabastro de perfume, se paró detrás de Él llorando, mojó Sus pies con sus lágrimas, los enjugó con sus cabellos, y derramó el perfume sobre Él. Esa mujer vino a adorar a Jesús. La adoración es la respuesta de un corazón limpio a un Rey santo.

blocks.en: 6. The King's Worship: Revival in the Hebrides
blocks.es_reference: 6. La Adoración del Rey: Avivamiento en las Hébridas

blocks.en: In the Hebrides Islands of Scotland, two elderly sisters, one eighty-four and the other eighty-two, had sought the face of God for revival for many years. Faith had reached a low point in their country. They claimed God's promise, "I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground" (Isaiah 44:3), and convinced their pastor that the people should ask God to quicken their hearts. He and a handful of men gathered in a barn to pray, three nights a week, month after month, with no results. Then one night a young deacon rose from his knees and read Psalm 24: "Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? … He who has clean hands and a pure heart." He said, "Brethren, we have been praying for months for revival, but I would like to ask: are our hearts clean? Is the heart pure?" In response they fell on their faces in confession and rededication and began to pray even more earnestly. By five o'clock that morning revival had come; the barn was filled with the glory of God, and the power that was let loose shook the whole community. The Lord brought to them the very man He was going to use — the Rev. Duncan Campbell. Within weeks the whole island was filled with a God-consciousness; churches overflowed; people who could not sleep came to church in the middle of the night to get right with God. In that Scottish community, not a home was left without someone coming to Christ.
blocks.es_reference: En las Islas Hébridas de Escocia, dos hermanas ancianas, una de ochenta y cuatro y la otra de ochenta y dos años, habían buscado el rostro de Dios por avivamiento durante muchos años. La fe había llegado a un punto bajo en su país. Reclamaron la promesa de Dios: "Yo derramaré aguas sobre el sequedal, y ríos sobre la tierra árida" (Isaías 44:3), y convencieron a su pastor de que el pueblo debía pedir a Dios que avivara sus corazones. Él y un puñado de hombres se reunieron en un granero a orar, tres noches por semana, mes tras mes, sin resultados. Entonces una noche un joven diácono se levantó de sus rodillas y leyó el Salmo 24: "¿Quién subirá al monte de Jehová? … El limpio de manos y puro de corazón." Dijo: "Hermanos, hemos orado por meses por avivamiento, pero quisiera preguntar: ¿están limpios nuestros corazones? ¿Es puro el corazón?" En respuesta cayeron sobre sus rostros en confesión y rededicación y comenzaron a orar aún más fervientemente. Para las cinco de la mañana el avivamiento había llegado; el granero se llenó de la gloria de Dios, y el poder que se soltó sacudió a toda la comunidad. El Señor les trajo al mismo hombre que iba a usar — el Rev. Duncan Campbell. En semanas toda la isla se llenó de una conciencia de Dios; las iglesias se desbordaban; gente que no podía dormir venía a la iglesia en mitad de la noche para reconciliarse con Dios. En aquella comunidad escocesa, no quedó un hogar sin que alguien viniera a Cristo.

blocks.en: 7. The King's Welcome
blocks.es_reference: 7. La Bienvenida del Rey

blocks.en: Psalm 24:7-8 (NKJV): "Lift up your heads, O you gates! And be lifted up, you everlasting doors! And the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 24:7-8 (RVG): "Alzad, oh puertas, vuestras cabezas, y alzaos vosotras, puertas eternas, y entrará el Rey de gloria. ¿Quién es este Rey de gloria? Jehová el fuerte y valiente, Jehová el poderoso en batalla."

blocks.en: At the end of the psalm, God is described as the King of glory, "the LORD strong and mighty." Inside the Ark of the Covenant were kept the Ten Commandments — all of which God's people had broken. But over those tablets of stone God had placed a cover, called the Mercy Seat. Every year, on the Great Day of Atonement, the High Priest would sacrifice a goat and sprinkle its blood upon that Mercy Seat. By means of that blood, the people's sins were hidden from God's eyes; the Lord did not see the broken commandments. Imagine what it meant to have that same ark go ahead of them into every battle — the Lord of free and faithful grace, who did not count their sins against them, marching on their side. God's great glory was best seen in the way He used His might on behalf of sinners. As David led the ark into Jerusalem, he wanted the city's gates opened as high and wide as they could possibly go, to take in every bit of God's glory.
blocks.es_reference: Al final del salmo, Dios es descrito como el Rey de gloria, "Jehová el fuerte y valiente." Dentro del Arca del Pacto se guardaban los Diez Mandamientos — todos los cuales el pueblo de Dios había quebrantado. Pero sobre aquellas tablas de piedra Dios había puesto una cubierta, llamada el Propiciatorio. Cada año, en el gran Día de la Expiación, el sumo sacerdote sacrificaba un macho cabrío y rociaba su sangre sobre aquel Propiciatorio. Por medio de esa sangre, los pecados del pueblo quedaban ocultos de los ojos de Dios; el Señor no veía los mandamientos quebrantados. Imagine lo que significaba que esa misma arca fuera delante de ellos a cada batalla — el Señor de la gracia libre y fiel, que no les tomaba en cuenta sus pecados, marchando a su lado. La gran gloria de Dios se veía mejor en la manera en que usaba Su poder a favor de los pecadores. Mientras David llevaba el arca a Jerusalén, quería que las puertas de la ciudad se abrieran tan altas y anchas como fuera posible, para recibir toda la gloria de Dios.

blocks.en: 8. No Room for the King
blocks.es_reference: 8. No Hubo Lugar para el Rey

blocks.en: The tragedy is that this glorious King is so often turned away. There was no room for Jesus at His birth. The Bethlehem innkeeper was not hostile and not opposed; his inn was simply crowded and his mind preoccupied. That is the answer millions give today. Their response to Christ is not atheism and not defiance; it is preoccupation — the feeling of being able to get on reasonably well without Him, every room in the heart already taken up by other crowding interests. There was no room for Jesus by His family or His nation either; He said, "Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head" (Matthew 8:20). One place always welcomed Him — the home in Bethany where Mary, Martha, and Lazarus lived.
blocks.es_reference: La tragedia es que a este Rey glorioso tan a menudo se le rechaza. No hubo lugar para Jesús en Su nacimiento. El mesonero de Belén no fue hostil ni se opuso; su mesón simplemente estaba lleno y su mente preocupada. Esa es la respuesta que millones dan hoy. Su respuesta a Cristo no es ateísmo ni desafío; es preocupación — la sensación de poder arreglárselas razonablemente bien sin Él, con cada cuarto del corazón ya ocupado por otros intereses que lo abarrotan. Tampoco hubo lugar para Jesús por parte de Su familia o Su nación; Él dijo: "Las zorras tienen guaridas, y las aves del cielo nidos; mas el Hijo del Hombre no tiene dónde recostar su cabeza" (Mateo 8:20). Un lugar siempre lo recibió — el hogar en Betania donde vivían María, Marta y Lázaro.

blocks.en: "It's Dark and Cold": A proud young woman lay dying. She had made room in her life for pleasure, fun, and sin, but no room for Jesus. As the shadows deepened she called to her father, "Papa, won't you go with me? It's so dark and cold." Her father replied, "Daughter, I can't go with you." Again she moaned, "It's dark and cold." Those were her last words. It will be dark and cold if we come to the end of this life without Christ. We may want the cards, the dance, and the world while we live; but we will want Christ at the last. (William Moses Tidwell, Effective Illustrations)
blocks.es_reference: "Está Oscuro y Frío": Una joven orgullosa yacía moribunda. Había hecho lugar en su vida para el placer, la diversión y el pecado, pero ningún lugar para Jesús. Al caer las sombras llamó a su padre: "Papá, ¿no irás conmigo? Está tan oscuro y frío." Su padre respondió: "Hija, no puedo ir contigo." De nuevo gimió: "Está oscuro y frío." Esas fueron sus últimas palabras. Estará oscuro y frío si llegamos al final de esta vida sin Cristo. Podemos querer las cartas, el baile y el mundo mientras vivimos; pero querremos a Cristo al final. (William Moses Tidwell, Effective Illustrations)

blocks.en: So David's psalm urges all of us: welcome your King. Seek His blessing and see His glory. Lift up the gates of your heart as high and wide as they will go, and let the King of glory come in.
blocks.es_reference: Así que el salmo de David nos exhorta a todos: dad la bienvenida a vuestro Rey. Buscad Su bendición y ved Su gloria. Alzad las puertas de vuestro corazón tan altas y anchas como puedan abrirse, y dejad entrar al Rey de gloria.

mc.stem: In what book and chapter is the story behind Psalm 24 — David bringing the Ark to Jerusalem — recorded?
options: 2 Samuel 6
1 Kings 8
Exodus 25
Joshua 6
mc.why: The story behind Psalm 24 is in 2 Samuel 6 — David bringing the Ark of God up to Jerusalem.

mc.stem: What had the Ark of the Covenant represented to Israel ever since Moses?
options: The wealth of the kingdom
The presence of God in the midst of His people
A trophy of war over the Philistines
The authority of the king
mc.why: Ever since Moses, the Ark represented the very presence of God dwelling in the midst of His people.

mc.stem: Why did the first attempt to bring the Ark to Jerusalem fail?
options: Uzzah reached out to steady the ark and died
A storm destroyed the cart
The Philistines attacked the procession
David lost his way to the city
mc.why: The first attempt failed when Uzzah reached out to steady the Ark and died — holiness cannot be handled carelessly.

mc.stem: Where was the Ark kept for three months after the first attempt failed?
options: In the tabernacle at Shiloh
Back among the Philistines
In David's own palace
In the house of Obed-Edom, who was blessed
mc.why: For three months the Ark stayed in the house of Obed-Edom, who was blessed because God's presence dwelt with him.

mc.stem: What is the most important question of the psalm, asked twice in its ten verses?
options: How long, O Lord?
Who is this King of glory?
Why do the nations rage?
What is man, that You are mindful of him?
mc.why: The psalm's great question, asked twice, is the one that matters most: 'Who is this King of glory?'

mc.stem: According to the lesson, the question "Who is this King of glory?" is answered in three ways. Which set is correct?
options: Creator, Redeemer, and Friend
Owner of the earth, Judge of His holy place, and the LORD strong and mighty
Father, Son, and Spirit
Prophet, Priest, and King
mc.why: The King of glory is answered three ways: Owner of the earth, Judge of His holy place, and the LORD strong and mighty.

mc.stem: What does "The earth is the LORD's, and all its fullness" teach about God?
options: That God is a good-luck charm to ward off trouble
That nature itself is divine
That He is the Owner and Creator of all things and all people
That the earth governs itself
mc.why: 'The earth is the LORD's' means God is Owner and Creator of all things and all people — nothing is outside His claim.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is mankind's true relationship to the earth?
options: We are the rightful owners of the earth
We may do with it whatever pleases us
The earth belongs to no one
We are tenant farmers and stewards, accountable to the Owner
mc.why: If the earth is the Lord's, we are tenant farmers and stewards, accountable to the Owner for what we hold.

mc.stem: Which Old Testament figure does the lesson cite as a faithful steward of another man's house?
options: Joseph, steward of Potiphar's house
Daniel in Babylon
Nehemiah the cupbearer
Elisha the prophet
mc.why: Joseph, set over Potiphar's house, is the picture of a faithful steward managing what belongs to another.

mc.stem: The image of a sharecropper, cited in the lesson, illustrates what about our relationship to God?
options: That we own nothing and owe God nothing
That the earth belongs to no one
That we are stewards working land that belongs to God, accountable to Him
That wealth is a sign of God's favor
mc.why: The sharecropper image teaches that we work land that belongs to God and remain accountable to Him for it.

mc.stem: What does 1 Timothy 6:7, quoted in the lesson, say about our possessions?
options: The laborer is worthy of his wages
Money is the root of all evil
We brought nothing into the world, and can carry nothing out
Sell all you have and give to the poor
mc.why: 1 Timothy 6:7 reminds us we brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out — we are stewards, not owners.

mc.stem: In the story of Achan (Joshua 7), what was the root of his sin and Israel's defeat?
options: He worshiped a foreign idol
He refused to fight at Jericho
He lied to Joshua about a vision
He took and hid what belonged to God
mc.why: Achan's sin and Israel's defeat came from taking and hiding what belonged to God — robbing the rightful Owner.

mc.stem: What is the central thesis connecting the King's World to worship?
options: If we work hard, God owes us blessing
Worship is optional for the busy
If the world is the Lord's, then He is worthy of our worship
The earth worships God on our behalf
mc.why: The thesis is simple: if the whole world is the Lord's, then He is worthy of our worship.

mc.stem: According to Psalm 24:3-5, who may ascend the hill of the LORD and stand in His holy place?
options: He who has clean hands and a pure heart
He who brings the largest offering
He who is born into the priestly line
He who has never been to battle
mc.why: Psalm 24 says only the one with clean hands and a pure heart may ascend God's hill and stand in His holy place.

mc.stem: What had David learned from Uzzah's death that applied to the King's Worship?
options: That oxen are unreliable
That holiness cannot be taken lightly when approaching God
That he should never dance before the LORD
That the ark should stay in Abinadab's house
mc.why: Uzzah's death taught David that holiness cannot be taken lightly when we approach a holy God.

mc.stem: In the lesson, which two examples are given of those who came to worship Jesus?
options: Peter and John
The rich young ruler and Nicodemus
The wise men, and the sinful woman with the alabaster jar

sa.prompt: Explain the historical event behind Psalm 24: why did the first attempt to bring the Ark to Jerusalem fail, and what does that failure teach about approaching God?
sa.model: The story behind Psalm 24 is David bringing the Ark of God up to Jerusalem in 2 Samuel 6. The first attempt failed because the Ark was carried on a new ox cart rather than as God had commanded; when the cart shook and Uzzah reached out to steady the Ark, he died. The Ark then stayed three months in the house of Obed-Edom, who was blessed, before David brought it up properly the second time. The lesson is that holiness cannot be handled carelessly; we must approach a holy God on His terms, with reverence, not on our own convenient ideas.

sa.prompt: What is the most important question of Psalm 24, and what are the three answers the psalm gives to it?
keywords_en: who is this King of glory
sa.model: The most important question of Psalm 24 is asked twice: "Who is this King of glory?" The psalm answers it three ways. First, He is the Owner of the earth and all its fullness, the Creator of all things and all people. Second, He is the Judge of His holy place, the One worthy to stand in His own sanctuary. Third, He is "the LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle," the victorious King. Together these answers show that the One who comes to us is the sovereign Owner, holy Judge, and conquering King of all.

sa.prompt: Explain "the King's World" (Psalm 24:1). What does it mean that the earth is the Lord's, and how does that define our role?
sa.model: "The earth is the LORD's, and all its fullness" (Psalm 24:1) means that God is the Owner and Creator of everything and everyone; nothing lies outside His rightful claim. This defines our role precisely: we are not owners but tenants and stewards, entrusted with what belongs to Him and accountable to Him for how we use it. Our money, our time, our abilities, even our very lives, are held in trust from the true Owner. To live rightly is to remember that we manage God's property, and one day we will give an account of our stewardship.

sa.prompt: Use the parable of the vineyard (Matthew 21:33) and Bill Carlson's "The Sharecropper" to explain our stewardship before God.
sa.model: Both the parable of the vineyard in Matthew 21 and Bill Carlson's picture of the sharecropper teach the same truth about our standing before God. In the parable, an owner plants a vineyard and lets it out to tenants who must render him his share of the fruit; they are workers on land that is not theirs. A sharecropper likewise farms another man's field and owes the owner an account of the harvest. So we work and live on what belongs to God, enjoying its use but never its ownership, and we remain accountable to Him for the fruit of our lives.

sa.prompt: What does the sin of Achan (Joshua 7) teach about taking what belongs to God, and how does it connect to Psalm 24's claim that the earth is the Lord's?
sa.model: At Jericho God commanded that everything be devoted to Him, but Achan secretly took a beautiful robe, silver, and gold, and hid them in his tent. Because of that hidden sin, Israel was defeated at Ai until the sin was uncovered and judged. The story teaches the seriousness of taking for ourselves what belongs to God, the very opposite of the stewardship Psalm 24 calls for. If the whole earth is the Lord's, then robbing Him, whether of devoted things, of our tithe, or of the honor due Him, is a grave matter, and hidden sin has consequences beyond ourselves.

sa.prompt: Explain "the King's Worship" (Psalm 24:3-5). What does God require of those who would ascend His hill, and why?
sa.model: "The King's Worship" in Psalm 24:3-5 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and stand in His holy place, and answers: "He who has clean hands and a pure heart." God requires not outward ritual but inward purity, clean conduct and a heart that is not given to idols or falsehood. The reason is the holiness of God Himself; as Uzzah's death showed, the holy God cannot be approached carelessly. We cannot worship acceptably while clinging to sin. This drives us at last to Christ, the only One with truly clean hands and a pure heart, in whom we may draw near.

sa.prompt: The Hebrides Revival of 1949 is tied to Psalm 24. What does that account teach about the connection between clean hands, a pure heart, and God drawing near?
sa.model: In the Hebrides Revival of 1949, believers gave themselves to prayer, and the turning point came when the words of Psalm 24 cut through: are our hands clean, is our heart pure? When the people stopped seeking revival as an experience and instead sought clean hands and a pure heart before God, His presence came down in power. The account teaches that God draws near to a people who deal honestly with their sin and long for holiness. Revival is not worked up by technique; it comes when hearts are cleansed and God Himself is sought above all.

sa.prompt: Explain "the King's Welcome" (Psalm 24:7-10). What was the Mercy Seat, and how did it reveal God's glory toward sinners?
sa.model: "The King's Welcome" in Psalm 24:7-10 calls the gates to lift up so the King of glory may come in. Inside the Ark lay the broken tablets of the law, but over them was a golden lid called the Mercy Seat, and on the Day of Atonement blood was sprinkled there. The blood came between God's eyes and the broken commandments, so that the people's sins were covered. In this the glory of God shines toward sinners: He is holy and His law is broken, yet through the blood He makes a way to receive us. It points forward to Christ, whose blood is our mercy seat.

sa.prompt: Using the Bethlehem innkeeper, explain why so many give "no room" to Jesus today, and what kind of response it is.
sa.model: The Bethlehem innkeeper had no room for Mary and Joseph, and the lesson uses him to picture how millions respond to Jesus today. Notice the innkeeper was not hostile; he did not drive them away in anger or defiance. He was simply preoccupied, his inn already crowded and his attention full, so there was no room. That is how most people refuse Christ, not by open rebellion but by a heart already crowded with other things, getting on with life without Him. The danger is not always hatred of Christ; often it is a busy heart that never makes room for the King.

sa.prompt: What warning about welcoming the King does the lesson draw from the dying young woman who said "it's dark and cold"?
sa.model: The lesson tells of a dying young woman who, having lived without Christ, said at the end, "it's dark and cold," with no welcome waiting for her. It is a solemn warning that giving "no room" to the King is not harmless neglect but has eternal weight. The time to welcome Christ is now, while the heart is still tender and the door of life still open; to put it off until the end may be to find the door has closed. The lesson urges us not to be like the innkeeper or the young woman, but to throw open the gates and let the King of glory come in.
